approach.label: Approach
approach.title: How a question becomes a thing.
approach.hint: Hover or click each step. Each project shows up at the stage it is at today.
approach.loop: The last step feeds the first

steps.title: Observe
steps.text: See what people do, not what they say they do.

techniques.name: Shadowing and immersion in the operation
techniques.text: Following real users through their day to spot the bottlenecks nobody sees.

techniques.name: Reading logs and real data
techniques.text: Digging into database records and recurring tickets (Softdesk) before drawing conclusions.

steps.title: Understand
steps.text: Find the real question under the request, and prove it matters.

techniques.name: 5 Whys and root cause
techniques.text: Going past the symptom the user asks about to find the structural problem.

techniques.name: Process mapping (as-is)
techniques.text: Drawing every current step of the process to find where it stalls or causes rework.

techniques.name: Conversations about the pain
techniques.text: Asking people who live the problem whether the pain exists, how much it weighs and how they handle it, before any solution.

steps.gate: I only move to a solution once the problem holds up.

steps.title: Experiment
steps.text: Build the smallest thing that could prove me wrong.

techniques.name: MVP and quick prototype
techniques.text: Testing the idea with as little code or interface as possible before investing weeks of work.

techniques.name: Hypothesis testing with users
techniques.text: Putting the prototype in the hands of the people who run the process and measuring whether it really saves time.

steps.gate: Only what survived the test goes on to be built.

steps.title: Build
steps.text: Turn what survived into something people can use.

techniques.name: Clean architecture and automation
techniques.text: Building for stability, clear business rules (SQL, Pascal Script, React/AI) and simple maintenance.

techniques.name: Incremental delivery
techniques.text: Shipping in parts to deliver value quickly without stopping the operation.

steps.title: Improve
steps.text: Ship, watch, adjust. Then look again.

techniques.name: Continuous monitoring
techniques.text: Following usage metrics, errors and real feedback after delivery.

techniques.name: Cyclical iteration
techniques.text: Feeding what was learned back into the Observe step.

steps.gate: What shows up here goes back to the Observe step.

home.greeting: Hi, I'm Tisco. I know a few things about Iury. What would you like to know?

chips.label: Who is Iury?
chips.answer: Systems Support at Giassi Supermercados, working with SQL, PL/SQL and Oracle. He studies Computer Science (UNESC) and Systems Analysis and Development (UNOPAR). He learns by building, and this site shows what he found.

chips.label: AI experience?
chips.answer: The fullest case is Koinonia, a live product built with AI. Iury defined the problem, wrote the directives, ran the build and tested the result. At work he uses AI to write rules and automations on the DOX platform.

chips.label: How to reach him?
chips.answer: By email, iuryumbelino1@gmail.com, or on LinkedIn (in/iuryumbelino). His GitHub is @Umbelino-dev. Taking you to the contact section.

home.fallback: I couldn't reach the model just now. Try one of the suggestions, or write to Iury.

koinonia.greeting: I've read this case study. Ask me why a Radar, how AI was used or what the audit found.

chips.label: Why a Radar?
chips.answer: Because an attendance list says who came, not where to start. The Radar ranks people by risk of drifting away and turns that into a care queue. Newcomers are not flagged as at risk.

chips.label: How was AI used?
chips.answer: AI wrote the code from a brief and plans Iury wrote. He directed every round, checked the result and tested it on desktop and mobile.

chips.label: What did the audit find?
chips.answer: Silent failures. Unpaginated reads would have broken the Radar past a thousand records. An inverted date filter hid people who needed care. And there were no tests. All fixed.
